author: Frederick Douglass
title: My Bondage and My Freedom
edition: New York and Auburn: Miller, Orton & Mulligan, 1855. UNC Documenting the American South transcription of the Rare Book Collection copy, call number E4499.D738; scanned title page and verso and source description identify the printing. All 79 selected paragraphs are taken directly from that transcription. Original wording, spelling, punctuation and paragraph boundaries retained; HTML entities decoded, page labels and running matter omitted, prose line wrapping joined. Inline italic markup is omitted without changing its words. No modern introduction is included. The library text holds the Editor's Preface (which carries Douglass's letter of July 2, 1855), Part I (Life as a Slave), Part II (Life as a Freeman) and the Appendix of speeches and letters, with the chapter synopses and the book's six asterisk footnotes in that range, kept in Project Gutenberg’s note form: “[*]” at the citing word and the note after the paragraph or heading that cites it as “[Footnote *: …]”, a note of several paragraphs (the bill of sale and deed of manumission) opened in its first and closed at the end of its last. Where the transcription sets a note in the middle of a paragraph, the paragraph is given whole and the note follows it; the title page, dedication, contents, Dr. James M'Cune Smith's Introduction, the illustrations and the publisher's advertisements at the end are omitted. Verse quotations keep their printed lines. The passages read by the Grade 11 calendar readings in Chapters VI–XI (blocks 106–117, 120–127, 130–137, 140–150, 156–159, 162–164 and 169–170) were compared word by word, punctuation included, with the OCR text of two copies of the 1855 printing (Internet Archive mybondagemyfreed00doug and mybondagemyfreed00douguoft) and, where they differed, the page images; four readings changed to the printed text: “death. This” (block 127, where the transcription had “death: This”), “Col Lloyd” (block 137, where it supplied “Col[.]”), “tow-linen” (block 141, “two-linen”), and the full stop after “chains” (block 109), which failed to print in the transcription’s copy and in mybondagemyfreed00doug but is clear in the Toronto copy, p. 99. The misprints “noes” for hoes (block 116) and “addresssed” (block 127) stand as printed. The passages read by the Grade 11 calendar readings in Chapters XII–XVII (blocks 173–178, 184–213, 219–242, 247–264, 267–275 and 278–300) were compared the same way; three readings changed to the printed text: “coversion” (block 233, a misprint the transcription had silently corrected to “conversion”), “than” (block 253, where the transcription had “that the snake”), and “Capt Auld” (block 273, where it supplied “Capt[.]”). The misprints “allluding” (block 173), “equaily” (block 187) and “incapahle” (block 227), and the missing opening quotation mark before “Is your master at the store?” (block 230), stand as printed. The passages read by the Grade 11 calendar readings in Chapters I–VI (blocks 26–28, 53–59, 77–89, 92–99 and 102–105) were compared the same way, capitals included; three readings changed: “if he pleases” (block 96, where the transcription had “if the pleases”), “thick tongues” (block 79, whose first letter failed to print in the transcription’s copy and in mybondagemyfreed00doug but is clear in the Toronto copy, p. 72), and the misprint “litttle” (block 84, which the transcription had silently corrected), which stands as printed. The transcription’s capitals for the printing’s small capitals (“IDOLS”, “WIVES”, block 54) are left as transcribed. The passages read by the Grade 11 holiday readings (blocks 304–312, the Christmas holidays in Chapter XVIII; 339–343, the New Year of 1836 in Chapter XIX; and 625–639, “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” in the Appendix) were compared the same way, with the page images of the Toronto copy deciding every difference; five readings changed to the printed text: “undeserving” (block 304, where the transcription had “underserving”), “his slave,--a slave for life” (block 339, comma restored), “manhood” (block 343, a word divided at a line end that the transcription gave as “man hood”), “inhuman” (block 636, likewise given as “in-human”) and “search out every abuse” (block 639, where it had “search our”). The misprint “strickly” (block 305) stands as printed.

rights.basis: The selected text is from the specifically identified Miller, Orton & Mulligan 1855 printing, outside the US copyright term in 2026. UNC source description gives publisher, year and physical-copy call number, links the scanned title page and verso, and explicitly labels the edition No Copyright in US. The modern digitization contributes transcription and markup; no modern editorial prose is reproduced. Every selected paragraph was extracted from this dated-witness transcription, replacing the variant PG202 text.

acquisition.method: UNC Documenting the American South HTML file. Took the Editor's Preface and everything from “Life as a Slave” to the end of the Appendix; removed the page-number anchors and rules (rejoining paragraphs split across pages with a space) and illustration placeholders; decoded entities; dropped inline markup (italics, colour) keeping its words; each footnote callout (a linked superscript asterisk) became “[*]”, and each note (the coloured block after it) became “[Footnote *: …]” in place of its printed “* ”, the two halves of a paragraph it interrupted being rejoined with a space before the note; collapsed whitespace and removed leading indentation; paragraphs with line breaks became stanzas, and a list became one paragraph with an item per line; HTML headings became level-2 headings, each chapter number joined with its title. Ten readings (blocks 79, 84, 96, 109, 127, 137, 141, 233, 253 and 273) were then corrected to the 1855 printing after collation (see edition). Blocks 304, 339, 343, 636 and 639 were corrected the same way on 2026-11-18 (see edition).
